annotation.title_clean: “This robot is dictating her next steps in life”: disability justice and relational AI ethics
annotation.title_en: “This robot is dictating her next steps in life”: disability justice and relational AI ethics
annotation.authors_or_issuer: van Toorn, G; Scully, JL; Gendera, S
annotation.summary_en: Peer-reviewed qualitative study using dialogue groups with disabled people in Australia to examine how they judge AI and automated decision-making as more or less just. Ethical judgments hinge on self-determination, caring relationships, recognition of identity, and the political-economic drivers of automation, supporting a disability-conscious relational AI ethics.
key_provisions_or_claims: Disabled people's ethical judgments of ADM depend on relational and situational context.
Self-determination, care relationships and identity recognition are central to perceived justice.
Misrecognition by biased systems is experienced as injustice; some hope machines reduce human stigma.
Political-economic drivers of automation shape ethical concerns.
Calls for a disability-conscious relational AI ethics that centres disabled voices.
